First, let's simplify the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{x}^{2} & >5{x}^{2}+14 \\ 7{x}^{2}-5{x}^{2} & >14 \\ 2{x}^{2} & >14 \\ {x}^{2} & >7\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can use either of two methods to solve the inequality.

*Method 1 - Solving an Absolute Value Equation*

Taking the square root of both sides of the inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & >7 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}} & >\sqrt{7} \\ |x| & >\sqrt{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the definition of absolute value, we must have 

$$
x<-\sqrt{7}\,\text{or}\,x>\sqrt{7}.
$$

So, the solution is $\,x\in (-\infty ,-\sqrt{7})\cup (\sqrt{7},\infty ).$

*Method 2 - Picturing a Quadratic Curve*

Starting from ${x}^{2}>7$ and moving all terms to the left-hand side, we reach

$$
{x}^{2}-7>0.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding parabola given by $y={x}^{2}-7$ and find its roots:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-7 & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =7 \\ x & =\pm \sqrt{7}\end{aligned}
$$

So the roots are $x=\pm \sqrt{7}.$ 

Since the leading coefficient of ${x}^{2}-7$ is positive, the parabola opens upward. Therefore, the solution to the given inequality ($y>0$) lies outside the roots (but does not include them).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13965374/assets/1eba3bc41624ea6fdd11468b53630fd8995541ff01548ec57a36dad271e375f8.png)

Therefore, the solution is $x\in (-\infty ,-\sqrt{7})\cup (\sqrt{7},\infty ).$
